title: A Systematic Review of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring and Optimal Sensor Placement

subsections.subsection_title: Historical Foundations of Damage Detection and Nondestructive Evaluation
subsections.content:
In recent decades, SHM systems have become increasingly popular worldwide due to decaying infrastructure, ever-increasing load demands on existing structures, and the construction of complex new systems. In an SHM system, changes in engineering structures, such as bridges and buildings, are monitored over time using periodic response measurements ref [1]ref [2]ref [3]ref [4]ref [5]. A typical monitoring system involves two major processes: (I) sensing, to measure structure-dependent data, and (II) data analysis, to identify features from the acquired data allowing the distinction between an undamaged and damaged structure. Ideally, an SHM system fulfills the following requirements: high sensitivity to low damage levels and different types of faults, the capability of continuous monitoring, insensitivity to loading conditions and environmental effects, robustness to measurement of noise, and low installation and maintenance costs. Table 1 outlines the five principal levels of health monitoring, i.e., damage detection, localization, classification, quantification, and prognosis. In general, SHM systems consist of four components: (I) data collection systems, (II) transmission subsystems, (III) information management databases, and (IV) health Research on SHM sensor technologies has been ongoing for decades ref [2], ref [3]. Recently, researchers have been increasingly interested in embedding sensors for SHM systems. In ref [13], Rocha et al. reviewed embedded sensors for SHM systems and discussed sensor characteristics, interactions between sensor materials and host materials, embedding procedures, acquired sensor data, and material behavior. Stoll et al. ref [14] evaluated the feasibility of embedding eddy current sensors in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) components for SHM. Environmental and operational conditions (EOCs) pose a significant challenge to SHM systems. For SHM in high-temperature settings, Dutta et al. ref [15] investigated developments, limitations, applications, and recent advancements in fiber Bragg grating and eddy current sensors. In ref [16], Simon et al. presented a reliable SHM strategy using radar sensors at 60 GHz embedded in a wind turbine blade and exposed to a defined environment in a climate chamber. Recently, Mieloszyk et al. ref [17] analyzed the possibility of embedding fiber Bragg grating sensors into additive manufacturing polymeric elements with temperature exposure (both elevated and sub-zero). In recent decades, researchers have discussed different aspects of smart monitoring concepts. Guzman-Acevedo et al. ref [18] demonstrated the application of global positioning system (GPS) receivers, smartphones, and accelerometers, integrated into a smart sensor system for the SHM of bridges. In ref [7], Hassani et al. emphasized two main areas relating to smart monitoring: advanced sensing technologies and advanced damage identification algorithms. In addition to highlighting the application of remote and wireless sensing, they showed that advanced data management and analysis techniques are key to managing and interpreting data obtained from monitoring systems.

Before choosing the type of SHM system, two main decision factors should be determined: (I) monitoring time frame and (II) monitoring scale. Depending on the time frame, a structure may be under short-term or long-term monitoring. subsections.subsection_title: Background and Scope of Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.content:
Optimization strategies have existed since the times of Cauchy, Newton, and Lagrange. Newton and Leibniz upgraded differential calculus strategies for system optimization. Bernoulli, Euler, and Lagrange developed the fundamentals and basic concepts of calculus of variations related to the minimization of objective functions. In constrained engineering optimization, unknown multipliers are added to problems. In honor of its inventor, Lagrange, it is named after him. In an unconstrained optimization engineering problem, Cauchy implemented the steepest descent technique. With the development of high-speed digital computers in the late twentieth century, complex optimization processes were implemented, allowing new optimization approaches to be developed. Following these advances, much literature was generated on optimization techniques. Optimization algorithms are based on the minimization (or maximization) of an objective function (also referred to as an Error function) E(x). This mathematical function depends on the model's internal learnable parameters, which provide the basis for calculating target values (Y) based on predictors (X). Different types of objectives can be minimized or maximized, including distance, cost, energy, weight, waste, raw material consumption, processing time, loss, conversion, profit, efficiency, yield, capacity, and utility. An intelligent optimization algorithm with a learning ability is called a learning-based intelligent optimization algorithm (LIOA). An extensive survey of LIOAs was carried out by Li et al. including statistical analysis, classification of LIOA learning methods, and applications of LIOAs in complex optimization scenarios.

Sensors are devices capable of detecting and recording inputs from the physical environment ref [5], ref [6]. The input can be heat, light, motion, pressure, moisture, or other environmental phenomena ref [5], ref [6]. The sensor output is generally a signal, such as a voltage measurement, that can be converted into a human-readable scale or recorded as a digital quantity, and displayed at the sensor location or sent electronically over a network for further analysis and processing ref [5], ref [6]. Specific characteristics of sensors include range, accuracy, sensitivity, stability, static and dynamic specifications, repeatability, compensation of EOC changes, and energy harvesting ref [5], ref [6]. An ideal sensor is sensitive to the measured property and insensitive to any other properties they might encounter in their application ref [5], ref [6].

In general, an SHM system involves continuously monitoring an engineering structure to identify and analyze changes in the structure's geometric and material properties over time ref [10], ref [11]. In the 1980s, different SHM strategies were developed for various applications, from offshore structures to bridges to aerospace systems. For each application, unique monitoring strategies were developed, focusing on the particular requirements of the structures. Adams et al. ref [67] published one of the first milestone papers in this field. The au-thors developed an innovative non-destructive testing (NDT) method based on vibration measurements. Using vibration data from the structure and a suitable theoretical model (acceptance function), it was shown that damage could be identified in a one-dimensional model, estimating its location and magnitude. During this time, Cawley et al. ref [68] realized that damage causes local stiffness reductions and changes in natural frequencies that can be used to locate the damage. Today's state-of-the-art in SHM aims to provide accurate and robust systems that can detect, locate, and estimate the size and type of damage and provide remaining lifetime estimations ref [11], ref [13]. The health assessment of a system involves identifying four system characteristics: ref [1] Environmental and operational conditions (EOCs), ref [2] Mechanical damage or fault, ref [3] Growth of fault or damage, and ref [4] System performance after damage or fault ref [10], ref [11].

SHM methods can be divided into two general categories: global and local ref [11], ref [12]. The importance of considering a global monitoring approach is often apparent when a specific structural component cannot be accessed, or the entire structure needs to be evaluated ref [10], ref [11]. Figure 5 displays various subdivisions of SHM systems. As can be seen in the figure, global monitoring can be subdivided into static and dynamic categories. Moreover, dynamic-based methods can be further divided into model-based and data-based methods. Data-based methodologies are based solely on measured data from monitoring systems and analytical rules to evaluate the structure and predict how a damage scenario will escalate over time or when a fault will occur ref [11], ref [13]. Model-based methods involve solving an inverse problem ref [10].

As stated above, an SHM system aims to continuously assess a structure to identify structural damage, including material damage and structural stability problems. Structural instability can occur due to joint displacements. The Degrees of Freedom (DOF) of joints are determined by their possible free movements or rotations, i.e., the number of directions in which the joints of a system can cause a displacement. Therefore, DOFs are good candidates for installing sensors to collect data for structural damage detection ref [5].

Static-Based As a traditional global SHM system, Frigui et al. ref [111] investigated a new vibrationbased damage detection method (VBDDM) to detect and localize damage. This method was tested on a finite element model of an existing building. In ref [112], a nonlinear vibroacoustic modulation technique was used for structural damage identification. To illustrate the proposed methodology, nonlinear vibro-acoustic responses from composites were simulated, and data from an impact test was used.

In optimization-oriented SHM system design, optimal sensor placement under physical and operational constraints has also been emphasized for advanced monitored systems ref [14], while derivative-free optimization provides a relevant methodological basis when objective functions are expensive or gradient information is unavailable ref [15].

Biology-based, or bioinspired, optimization algorithms are called memetic algorithms, due to their analogy with biological evolution and activity. The algorithms can be subdivided into two categories: trajectory-based algorithms and population-based algorithms. Population-based algorithms are also referred to as evolutionary algorithms (EAs). EAs are search methods that mimic biological evolution processes and species' social behaviors. The subsequent generation surpasses the parents of algorithms through learning, evaluation, and adaptation. Among them, GA and its variations are the most common algorithms.

In 1995, Kennedy and Eberhart proposed an evolutionary computation method called PSO ref [189]. In this algorithm, every solution is considered a bird flock particle. Accordingly, in addition to individual intelligence, the birds show extended social behaviors and coordinate their movement to a specific goal. Initially, random positions and velocities are assumed for each particle in the search space. In addition to the optimization methodologies presented above, researchers developed and employed various other techniques to detect damage and find optimized sensor configurations. For instance, an optimization strategy called Snobfit ref [260] was designed by Guratzsch ref [19] to optimize noisy objective functions under bound constraints. In ref [261], a novel approach to detecting damage to trusses, space frames, and plate structures was presented by combining Bayesian data fusion with teaching-learning-based optimization (TLBO) algorithms. The Kalman filter algorithm ref [262], which estimates state vectors and the variances of errors, was utilized in combination with sequential placement strategies for addressing OSP problems in ref [263]. In ref [264], a forward sub-structuring approach, modal strain energy, and the enhanced bat algorithm (EBA) were utilized in an effective threestage method for detecting damage in large-scale space structures. Additionally, a variety of other methodologies are also available for OSP, such as the following: energy-efficient sensor deployment ref [265], backup sensor-based fault-tolerance SHM method ref [266], mixed variable pattern search algorithm ref [267], frequency domain-based OSP technique ref [268], three-phase sensor placement approach ref [269], Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure ref [270], e-Estimator algorithms ref [271], and wave propagation-based local interaction simulation approach ref [272]. SHM problems can also be analyzed using other computational methodologies, including the guided water strider algorithm ref [273], grasshopper optimization algorithm (GOA) ref [274], improved imperialist competitive algorithm ref [275], atom search algorithm (ASO) ref [276], equilibrium optimizer algorithm ref [277], grey wolf optimizer algorithm ref [278], balancing composite motion optimization ref [279], Q-learning evolutionary algorithm ref [280], Kriging-particle swarm optimization algorithm ref [281], and topology optimization ref [282]. More details of these methodologies can be found in the associated studies.

An information entropy based sensor placement method for structural damage detection and benchmark SHM applications was also proposed for optimizing vibration sensor configurations ref [17].

The Effective Independence (EI) method is one of the most widely used OSP methods for modal testing and was proposed by Kammer, as also noted in later OSP comparisons based on Tabu search algorithms ref [6]. It is an iterative method based on the Fisher matrix (FIM), providing information about unknown parameters of a sampled random variable ref [22] ref [6]. Fisher information refers to the variance of the score regarding the unknown parameter. Multiple unknown parameters can be expressed using these matrices and their elements ref [22]. Among classical metaheuristics, simulated annealing has been widely adopted for combinatorial optimization and provides a general foundation for OSP search procedures ref [19]. Improved simulated annealing has also been specifically developed for optimal sensor placement using objective functions such as the determinant of the FIM, MAC, and MSE of mode shapes ref [22]. Likewise, Tabu search has been introduced directly for OSP in structural health monitoring and compared against ECEFI and EI under MAC-, Fisher-matrix-, condition-number-, and LMSE-based criteria ref [6]. Related tabu-search-based metaheuristic developments for vibration-based structural damage identification further support the use of reactive or hybrid tabu strategies in multimodal structural optimization problems ref [5].

Physics-based algorithms are heuristic algorithms that mimic matter's physical properties or physical behavior ref [7]. These algorithms include Simulated Annealing (SA), Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA), Electromagnetism-Like Algorithm (EMA), Particle Collision Algorithm (PCA), and Gravitation Field Algorithm (GFA). Below, SA is discussed in more detail. The reader is referred to ref [239]ref [240]ref [241] for a comprehensive overview of other physics-inspired optimization techniques.

Optimization algorithms are further used in AI technologies, such as ANN ref [337], ML ref [338], and DL ref [339], to optimize and automatically improve the learning. As such, a neural network optimizer changes attributes of the network, such as weights and learning rate, to reduce losses. The first step in solving a neural network problem is to define a loss function. Optimization algorithms and strategies are used to minimize losses to provide the most accurate results. Different types of optimizers to reduce the loss function include the following: gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (MB-SGD), SGD with momentum, Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG), adaptive gradient (AdaGrad), AdaDelta, RMSprop, and Adam.

In optimization context, benchmarking and algorithm-selection perspectives are important because no single optimizer performs best across all problems ref [7], and algorithm selection therefore depends on problem characteristics and landscape features ref [23], ref [25]. Test and benchmark functions are commonly used to validate and compare optimization algorithms, and useful benchmark suites should cover diverse properties such as modality, separability, and landscape structure ref [26]. In noisy settings, theoretical comparisons of direct-search and derivative-free strategies also show that algorithm behavior can differ substantially under uncertainty, reinforcing the need for problem-aware benchmarking and selection ref [24].

subsections.content:
The KE approach is based on the principle that if any sensor is placed at a point of maximum KE, the sensor has maximum ability to measure the modes of interest ref [32], ref [7]. Possible sensor locations are ranked, based on their dynamic contribution to the target mode shapes ref [28], ref [7]. There is a critical difference between this method and the EI method, i.e., instead of analyzing the FIM determinant, a KE measure is maximized here ref [28], ref [6], ref [7]. Engineering literature refers to this method as the kinetic energy method (KEM) or modal kinetic energy (MKE) ref [32], ref [7]. As introduced in Section 1.1, optimization procedures can be employed to optimize processes in many different disciplines, including civil, mechanical, power, medical, chemical, electrical, electronics, and industrial engineering ref [29], ref [32], ref [6]. Optimization Algorithms (OAs) help reduce the cost and risk of engineering design and operation and are applied to the design of multi-phase reactors, flow systems, SHM systems, neural networks, sensor detection systems, image processing, or manufacturing processes ref [29], ref [32], ref [6]. The concept of optimization can be explained in several ways:

GA is based on Darwin's theory of selection and evolution ref [213]. The features used in this optimization are genes, chromosomes, and population. A gene is an individual characterized by a set of parameters (variables). A chromosome is formed by joining genes into a string (solution). A population is composed of individuals who are the starting point of the process.

Geography-based optimization is a metaheuristic algorithm that generates random solutions in the geographical search space. The imperialistic competition algorithm (ICA) and Tabu Search (TS) are examples of these algorithms. A defining characteristic of TS is that it generates an updated list of solutions that are not allowed. Further, a critical factor is considered that relaxes the optimization criteria if no better solutions exist. In this way, local minima can be overcome. The TS flowchart is shown in Figure 16, and Table 13 summarizes the advantages and disadvantages of TS. Arafa et al. ref [252] developed a hybrid optimization approach that included two components: modified continuous reactive TS (MCRTS) and real-coded GAs. The algorithm was tested on several beam structures with crack damage, and the natural frequencies were used as features. After several runs, the developed algorithm consistently found the two sought-for optima. In ref [253], a TS heuristic was proposed to solve both economic criteria and critical variables for the optimal design and upgrading of sensors ref [29]. Two industrial process networks were compared for their performance using stochastic solution strategies ref [29]. A TS-based routing algorithm (TSRA) was proposed by Orojloo et al. ref [254] for determining the optimal route from a source to a destination in WSNs. This algorithm integrated energy consumption and hopped counts into routing decisions using a new move and neighborhood search method. The TSRA obtained more balanced transmission among nodes, reduced energy consumption and routing costs, and extended the network's lifetime for different randomly generated networks. It was shown in ref [255] that the TS algorithm could be used for the OSP problem in moving force identification. Some numerical simulations were conducted on a 2D planar truss model to evaluate a proposed TS-based OSP procedure. An optimization objective function was defined as the MAC matrix's mean values of off-diagonal elements ref [32], ref [7]. The TS-based OSP approach was found to be feasible and more accurate compared to previous methods ref [32], ref [7].

DE is a population-based metaheuristic search algorithm that iteratively improves a candidate solution based on an evolutionary process ref [36]. This algorithm was first presented by Storn and Price ref [219] in 1997. There are three real control parameters in this optimization algorithm: ref [1] crossover constant C r, ref [2] differentiation constant F, and ref [3] population size. Other parameters include:

In general, meta-heuristic algorithms use low computational power but require a long time to reach an optimal solution ref [34], ref [35], ref [9]. Hence, they are designed to find a solution that is "good enough" in a time that is "small enough" ref [36], ref [9]. Likewise, sequential sensor placement (SSP) algorithms are computationally efficient but may require a long time to determine the true global optimum from the obtained solution ref [33], ref [34]. Iterative algorithms, such as SSP, optimize error functions by adding or removing a subset of candidates in each iteration. In cases where the candidates are sequentially removed, the algorithms are termed backward sequential sensor placement (BSSP), while in cases where they are added, they are termed forward sequential sensor placement (FSSP) ref [256].

This study systematically reviewed the application of optimization algorithms (OAs) for structural health monitoring (SHM) and optimal sensor placement (OSP) ref [40], ref [41], ref [42], ref [43]. The integration of optimization methodologies for monitoring strategies is essential for the design of cost-effective and reliable systems. The paper provided a comprehensive overview of current SHM and OSP techniques. It included problem definitions and critical discussions on the advantages and disadvantages of the principal methodologies and suitable applications ref [40], ref [41], ref [42]. The state-of-the-art optimization algorithms were presented, including biology-based algorithms ref [40], ref [42], physics-based algorithms ref [43], geography-based algorithms, and sequential placement algorithms. Since evolutionary algorithms outperform other methods when addressing combinational methodologies, such as OSP, the most widely used evolutionary algorithms, and their most recently improved variants were summarized ref [40], ref [41], ref [42]. Using machine learning algorithms in SHM and OSP is an emerging technology with many advantages over traditional approaches. As a final note, the study discussed the suitability of computational methods for specific OSP and SHM applications, where evolutionary algorithms are used more commonly ref [40], ref [41], ref [42], ref [43]. Numerous summary tables were provided as a guide for the reader to solve SHM and OSP problems using the most suitable optimization methodology.
